'''Teresa Kaye Woodruff''' is an American [[Academic administration|university administrator]] and medical researcher in [[human reproduction]] and [[oncology]], with a focus on ovarian biology, endocrinology, and women's health. She is President Emerita<ref>{{Cite web |title=President Emerita |url=https://trustees.msu.edu/meetings/documents/2024/AA1-Emerita%20Designations%202%20STAMP.pdf}}</ref> of [[Michigan State University]], having served as interim president from 2022 to 2024.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |title=MSU trustees name Teresa K. Woodruff interim president |url=https://msutoday.msu.edu/news/2022/trustees-unanomously-approve-woodruff-interim-president |access-date=October 31, 2022 |publisher=Michigan State University}}</ref> Woodruff initially joined [[Michigan State University]] as the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs in 2020.<ref name=":2">{{cite web|url=https://msutoday.msu.edu/news/2020/woodruff-takes-office-as-provost|title=Woodruff takes office as provost|date=2020-08-03|publisher=MSU Today|access-date=2022-10-13}}</ref>  In 2025, she was a recipient of the [[National Medal of Science]], the first person from Michigan State University to receive the honor.<ref name="National Medal of Science">{{cite web |author=The White House |date=3 January 2025 |title=President Biden Honors Nation's Leading Scientists, Technologists, and Innovators |url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2025/01/03/president-biden-honors-nations-leading-scientists-technologists-and-innovators/ |access-date=4 January 2025 |website=The White House}}</ref><ref name=":0">https://msutoday.msu.edu/news/2025/national-medal-of-science-awarded-to-tkw</ref>

Woodruff was previously Dean of the Graduate School and Professor in the McCormick School of Engineering at Northwestern University.<ref name="provost">{{Cite web |last=Pollard |first=James |date=2020-04-27 |title=TGS Dean Teresa Woodruff named provost at Michigan State University |url=https://dailynorthwestern.com/2020/04/27/campus/teresa-woodruff-the-graduate-school-dean-named-provost-at-michigan-state/ |access-date=2020-10-30 |website=The Daily Northwestern}}</ref> She served as the Thomas J. Watkins Memorial Professor and Vice Chair for Research and Chief of the Division of Reproductive Science in Medicine in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at the [[Feinberg School of Medicine]] at [[Northwestern University]] in [[Chicago]], [[Illinois]].

Woodruff is credited with coining the term ''[[oncofertility]]'' and founded the [[Oncofertility Consortium]] at [[Northwestern Memorial Hospital]]. She is also founder and chief of the Division of Fertility Preservation and founder and director of the Women's Health Research Institute at Northwestern University.

In 2026, she was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] and the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite web |title=MSU Research Foundation Distinguished Professor Dr. Teresa K. Woodruff Elected to the Royal Society and the American Philosophical Society |url=https://msufoundation.org/msu-research-foundation-distinguished-professor-dr-teresa-k-woodruff-elected-to-the-royal-society-and-the-american-philosophical-society/ |publisher=MSU Research Foundation}}</ref>

== Education ==
Woodruff graduated with a Bachelor of Science degree in Zoology and Chemistry from the [[Olivet Nazarene University]] in 1985. She was awarded the "O" Award in 2016, presented "to honor alumni who exhibit the characteristics and ideals of their alma mater."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.olivet.edu/alumni-awards-past-recipients|title=Alumni Awards Past Recipients {{!}} Olivet Nazarene University|website=www.olivet.edu|date=September 2017|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> She completed her graduate study at [[Northwestern University]], receiving a Ph.D. in Molecular Biology and Cell Biology in 1989. She was recognized by Northwestern with their highest honor for an alum, the Northwestern Alumni Association Merit Award in 2012.<ref>https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2012/03/northwestern-alumni-association-awards/</ref>

She is the recipient of two honorary degrees (''Honorary Scientiae Doctoris'', i.e., D.Sc.), nationally from Bates College in Lewiston Maine (2010)<ref>https://www.bates.edu/president/honorary-degrees/list-of-honorary-degree-recipients/</ref> and internationally from University of Birmingham, School of Medicine in Birmingham, UK (2016).<ref>https://www.birmingham.ac.uk/university/colleges/mds/alumni/our-alumni/honorary-graduates</ref>

== Career ==
===Ovarian biology research===
In 1986, as a graduate student in the laboratory of Kelly Mayo at Northwestern University, Woodruff cloned the protein subunits that form the peptide hormones [[Activin and inhibin|inhibin and activin]]. This work was recognized in 2000 by the Endocrine Society Weitzman Award, which is presented to "an exceptionally promising young clinical or basic investigator who has not reached the age of 50."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.endocrine.org/awards/laureate-awards/richard-e-weitzman-outstanding-early-career-investigator-award|title=Richard E. Weitzman Outstanding Early Career Investigator Award {{!}} Endocrine Society|website=www.endocrine.org|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>  After completing her doctorate in 1989, Woodruff completed a postdoctoral fellowship at [[Genentech|Genentech, Inc]] in South San Francisco, CA, where she contributed to the development of inhibin and activin assays, which are used today for the diagnosis of [[Down syndrome]] and to measure the [[ovarian reserve]]. She is named as inventor on five patents based on her work at Genentech. Woodruff also continued her research into the physiology of inhibin and activin in pituitary and ovarian function in rodent and the effects of recombinant human inhibin and activin in primates.

Woodruff returned to Northwestern University as a faculty member in 1995 to study inhibin and activin actions and interactions within the pituitary-gonadal axis, characterizing the regulation of subunit assembly and ligand processing in the ovary, the ligands' role in [[Paracrine signaling|paracrine]] regulation of [[folliculogenesis]], and their [[signal transduction]] pathways in the regulation of [[follicle-stimulating hormone]] (FSH). In collaboration with Theodore Jardetzky, she solved the crystal structures of activin with its receptor and with its bioneutralizing binding protein [[follistatin]]. In 2015, her lab used ''in silico'' methods to design small molecule activin antagonists based on the structure of activin bound to its receptor.

Using single-cell elemental analytical methods at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in collaboration with inorganic chemist Tom O'Halloran, Woodruff discovered a role of [[zinc]] in the regulation of [[oocyte]] maturation and at the moment of [[Fertilisation|fertilization]]. Using single-cell [[x-ray fluorescence]], Woodruff and O'Halloran described the phenomenon of the "zinc spark," an event during which 10 billion zinc ions are lost from the egg. The discovery of the zinc spark was named as one of ''Discove''r magazine's top 100 stories of 2016.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2017/janfeb/47-spark-of-life|title=Spark of Life {{!}} DiscoverMagazine.com|website=Discover Magazine|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

===Oncofertility research===
[[File:Obama with the 2010 awardees for the Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentoring.jpg|thumb|Woodruff (right) with President [[Barack Obama]], representing an organizational recipient of the 2010 Presidential Awards for Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentoring<ref name="nsfedu">{{cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=122273|title=President Obama Honors Outstanding Science, Math and Engineering Mentors|last1=Zacharias|first1=Maria|date=December 14, 2011|website=NSF.gov|publisher=National Science Foundation|language=en|access-date=August 20, 2018|quote=Women's Health Science Program for High School Girls and Beyond, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Ill., represented by Teresa Woodruff|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180820172927/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=122273|archive-date=August 20, 2018|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>]]

At Northwestern University, Woodruff led a highly collaborative effort that resulted in the development of a [[Gel|hydrogel]] that acts as a 3-dimensional support system for encapsulated in vitro culture of the [[ovarian follicle]] and its enclosed maturing oocyte (eIVFG). Live births in mice resulted from these studies, and this work was named as the most important breakthrough of the decade 1998-2008 by ''Nature Medicine''. eIVFG methods were subsequently used to develop and test a microfluidic system that supports 28-day reproductive cycles ''ex vivo''—an "ovarian cycle in a dish."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kesq.com/lifestyle/healthy_living/cycle-in-a-dish-explores-female-intricacies/573381340|title='Cycle in a Dish' Explores Female Intricacies|date=2017-07-03|website=KESQ|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> On March 28, 2017, her team announced the creation of Evatar, a miniaturized [[Female reproductive system|female reproductive tract]] composed of ovarian follicles or intact ovaries (mouse) interconnected with human explants from fallopian tubes, uterus, and cervix with liver organoids to provide a metabolic management tissue system.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://futurism.com/a-new-menstrual-biochip-could-revolutionize-treatments-for-reproductive-diseases|title=A New Menstrual Biochip Could Revolutionize Treatments For Reproductive Diseases|website=Futurism|date=March 30, 2017 |language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/2017/03/scientists-build-menstrual-biochip-everything-bleed/|title=Scientists Build a Menstrual Biochip That Does Everything But Bleed|last=Molteni|first=Megan|date=2017-03-28|magazine=Wired|access-date=2019-04-14|issn=1059-1028}}</ref> Woodruff and team also recently created decellularized and 3D-printed ovarian bioprosthetics as replacement organs for women who have lost gonadal function.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stuff.co.nz/life-style/parenting/pregnancy/92713274/fresh-hope-for-infertile-women-after-live-births-using-3dprinted-ovaries|title=Fresh hope for infertile women after live births using 3D-printed ovaries|website=Stuff|date=May 17, 2017|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> The development of an ovarian bioprosthetic was named as one of ''Discover'' magazine's 100 most important discoveries of 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://discovermagazine.com/2018/janfeb/36-mice-birth-pups-from-artificial-ovaries|title=Mice Birth Pups From Artificial Ovaries {{!}} DiscoverMagazine.com|website=Discover Magazine|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> and was recognized as a top five medical breakthrough by the Chinese Academy of Science. Her work to bridge the basic sciences and medicine was recognized with a Halo Award in 2018.<ref>{{Cite press release|url=https://www.newswire.com/news/halo-honors-chicagos-heroes-of-medicine-20688947|title=Halo Honors Chicago's 'Heroes of Medicine'|website=www.newswire.com|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

In 2006, Woodruff introduced the term ''[[oncofertility]]'' to describe the application of her work to meeting the fertility needs of young cancer patients<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,2022642,00.html|title=Fertility and Cancer: Surviving and Having Kids Too|last=Rochman|first=Bonnie|date=October 11, 2010|magazine=Time|access-date=August 8, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160911084322/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,2022642,00.html|archive-date=September 11, 2016|url-status=live|language=en-US|issn=0040-781X|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2013-01-30/news/ct-x-cancer-fertility-20130130_1_cancer-patients-fertile-hope-young-women|title=Cancer and kids: Young women explore fertility options|last=Bowen|first=Alison|date=February 1, 2016|work=Chicago Tribune|access-date=August 13, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180813044105/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2013-01-30/news/ct-x-cancer-fertility-20130130_1_cancer-patients-fertile-hope-young-women|archive-date=August 13, 2018|language=en|df=mdy-all}}</ref> and she has "been at the center of the movement ever since."<ref name="ref1e0ae3">{{cite web|url=http://btn.com/2015/09/27/btn-livebig-northwestern-brightens-future-for-female-cancer-patients/|title=BTN LiveBIG: Northwestern brightens future for female cancer patients|last=Rindner|first=Grant|date=September 27, 2015|website=Big Ten News|access-date=September 27, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150927211522/http://btn.com/2015/09/27/btn-livebig-northwestern-brightens-future-for-female-cancer-patients/|archive-date=September 27, 2015|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref> With a $21.5-million [[National Institutes of Health]] Interdisciplinary Roadmap Grant awarded in 2007, she launched the [[Oncofertility Consortium]], an interdisciplinary team of oncologists, fertility specialists, social scientists, educators, and policy makers dedicated to the clinical care of women at risk of losing their fertility because of cancer treatment. As part of the Oncofertility Consortium, Dr. Woodruff helped form the National Physicians Cooperative (NPC) to facilitate sharing of fertility preservation protocols and techniques between reproductive endocrinology practices and ensure that clinicians and patients receive up-to-date information about available treatment options.

===Educational work===
Woodruff has provided leadership in higher education for over 25 years. She was selected by the Michigan State University (MSU) Board of Trustees to serve as interim president in 2022.<ref name=":1" /> As chief executive of MSU, Woodruff focused on advancing the university's strategic initiatives, building trust, enabling excellence, and affirming transparency, clarity, and authenticity. She led multiple university strategic plans, including: MSU 2030: Empowering Excellence, Advancing Equity, and Expanding Impact;<ref>{{Cite web |title=MSU 2030 Strategic Plan |url=https://strategicplan.msu.edu/strategic-plan |website=Michigan State University |language=en}}</ref> the Relationship Violence and Sexual Misconduct Plan;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Do more {{!}} Culture of Support {{!}} Michigan State University |url=https://supportmore.msu.edu/do-more |access-date=2025-03-25 |website=supportmore.msu.edu |language=en}}</ref> and the University Facilities and Use Strategic Plan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=University Facilities and Land Use Plan {{!}} Infrastructure Planning and Facilities |url=https://ipf.msu.edu/campus-plan |website=ipf.msu.edu}}</ref> Her vision shifted the admissions process from 'major' to 'mission' and she enhanced the financial aid processes including approval of the Spartan Tuition Advantage program, offering financial aid that covers the full cost of tuition for qualifying students (~6000) from the state of Michigan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New MSU program will eliminate tuition costs for eligible students starting next year |url=https://statenews.com/article/2023/10/new-msu-program-will-eliminate-tuition-costs-for-eligible-students-starting-next-year |access-date=October 9, 2023 |website=The State News |language=en-us}}</ref> She also led the most ambitious expansion of physical spaces at the institution in decades, including a new teaching and learning dairy, greenhouses, the MSU Museum, a new plant science building, a multi-dimensional a multicultural center, a student-focused health and wellness center and an engineering and digital innovation center (EDIC).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Building space for innovation at MSU |url=https://msutoday.msu.edu/news/2024/Building-space-for-innovation-MSU |website=MSUToday {{!}} Michigan State University |language=en}}</ref> MSU was also been recognized during Woodruff's term with its largest one-year leap in U.S. News and World Report rankings (17 places upward)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Michigan State jumps ahead in annual college ranking |url=https://www.lansingstatejournal.com/story/news/2023/09/19/michigan-state-us-news-world-report-best-colleges-ranking/70902925007/ |access-date=September 19, 2023 |website=Lansing State Journal}}</ref> and named a top 14 public institution by ''The Wall Street Journal''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wall Street Journal ranking recognizes MSU student outcomes |url=https://msutoday.msu.edu/errors/500?error=%2fnews%2f2023%2fwall-street-journal-ranking-recognizes-msu-student-outcomes |access-date=September 25, 2023 |website=MSUToday {{!}} Michigan State University |language=en}}</ref>

Prior to serving as interim president, Woodruff was named provost and executive vice president for academic affairs at MSU in 2020.<ref name=":2" /> Woodruff was responsible for the academic progression of over 51,000 students, the professional development of over 5,600 faculty and academic staff, and a multi-billion-dollar budget.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Facts |url=https://msu.edu/about/facts |website=Michigan State University |language=en}}</ref>

Prior to MSU, Woodruff served in governance roles for multiple societies, including as president of the Endocrine Society and on the council of the Society for the Study of Reproduction. She has held multiple senior academic roles including as associate provost of graduate education and dean of the Graduate School at Northwestern University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Teresa Woodruff named dean of The Graduate School |url=https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2017/august/teresa-woodruff/ |access-date=August 18, 2017 |website=news.northwestern.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Woodruff was named director of the newly formed Institute for Women's Health Research at Northwestern University, where she spearheaded advocacy and education on sex equity in biomedical research, the attrition of women from STEM fields, and the need for greater knowledge of basic science concepts among patients. Her call for sex equity in clinical trials was the subject of a 2014 interview with Lesley Stahl on ''60 Minutes''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/sex-matters-drugs-can-affect-sexes-differently/|title=Sex matters: Drugs can affect sexes differently|website=www.cbsnews.com|date=February 9, 2014 |language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

Woodruff also created the Women's Health Science Program (WHSP) for High School Girls & Beyond to provide science education programs to 9th -12th grade female students in Chicago Public Schools. WHSP runs four academies: the Oncofertility Saturday Academy (OSA), Cardiology Summer Academy (CSA), Infectious Disease Summer Academy (IDSA), and Physical Science Weekend Academy (PSWA). For this work, Woodruff was awarded the Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics, and Engineering Mentoring in an Oval Office ceremony in 2011.<ref name="nsfedu" />

Woodruff created a series of videos for 8- to 12-year-olds covering topics such as puberty, menstruation, and anatomy; a MOOC for college students on reproductive health;<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://abc7chicago.com/1006283/|title=Northwestern offers Sex 101 for freshmen, public|date=2015-09-28|website=ABC7 Chicago|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> and the Repropedia, a dictionary of reproductive science and health terms, created and updated by science and clinician contributors, for links to websites and social media to ensure accurate understanding of key terms by the public.<ref name="Stevens 2018">{{Cite news|url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/lifestyles/ct-sex-ed-college-students-northwestern-balancing-0929-20150929-column.html|title=Birds, bees and beers: Sex Ed 101 arrives at Northwestern|last=Stevens|first=Heidi|date=September 29, 2015|work=Chicago Tribune|access-date=August 8, 2018|language=en-US|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180808171353/http://www.chicagotribune.com/lifestyles/ct-sex-ed-college-students-northwestern-balancing-0929-20150929-column.html|archive-date=August 8, 2018|url-status=live|df=mdy-all}}</ref>

In 2015, Woodruff was named the Director of the Center for Reproductive Science at Northwestern University. In 2016, she founded the Masters of Science in Reproductive Science and Medicine program within the Center.

=== Awards and recognition ===
In 2025, Woodruff was a recipient of the [[National Medal of Science]], the first person from Michigan State University to receive the honor.<ref name="National Medal of Science" /><ref name=":0" /> This was her second White House honor, having previously received the Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentoring from President Barack Obama in 2010.<ref name="nsfedu" /> She was awarded the  Women's Health Visionary Award by the Society for Women's Health Research (SWHR) in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-08 |title=Teresa Woodruff to receive "Women's Health Visionary Award" from Society for Women's Health Research |url=https://innovationcenter.msu.edu/teresa-woodruff-recieves-womens-health-visionary-award/ |access-date=2025-05-10 |website=innovationcenter.msu.edu |language=en-US}}</ref>

Woodruff holds 20 U.S. Patents. In 2017, she received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Award]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.feinberg.northwestern.edu/2017/04/woodruff-receives-guggenheim-fellowship/|title=Woodruff Receives Guggenheim Fellowship|website=news.feinberg.northwestern.edu|date=April 18, 2017|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> and was elected to the [[National Academy of Inventors]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mccormick.northwestern.edu/news/articles/2017/12/three-professors-named-to-national-academy-of-inventors.html|title=Three Professors Named to National Academy of Inventors|website=Northwestern Engineering|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> She was elected as a fellow to the [[National Academy of Medicine]] in 2018,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://dailynorthwestern.com/2018/10/16/campus/teresa-woodruff-the-graduate-school-dean-elected-to-national-academy-of-medicine/|title=The Graduate School Dean Teresa Woodruff is elected to National Academy of Medicine|last=Closson|first=Troy|date=2018-10-16|website=The Daily Northwestern|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> and to the American Academy of Arts & Sciences in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Teresa K. Woodruff |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/teresa-k-woodruff |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences}}</ref> Woodruff is also an elected Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2005<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Science|first=American Association for the Advancement of|date=2005-10-28|title=AAAS News and Notes|journal=Science|language=en|volume=310|issue=5748|pages=634–637|doi=10.1126/science.310.5748.634|issn=0036-8075|doi-access=}}</ref> as well as the [[American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aimbe.org/teresa-k-woodruff-ph-d-to-be-inducted-into-medical-and-biological-engineering-elite/|title=Teresa Woodruff Teresa K. Woodruff, Ph.D. To be Inducted into Medical and Biological Engineering Elite - AIMBE|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> She was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] and the [[American Philosophical Society]]<ref>{{cite web |author=Erin Farrell |date=May 1, 2026 |title=APS Elects 2026 Class of New Members |website=American Philosophical Society |url=https://www.amphilsoc.org/news/aps-elects-2026-class-new-members}}</ref> in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-05-27|title=Exceptional scientists elected as Fellows of the Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2026/05/new-fellows-announcement-2026/|access-date=2026-05-31|website=Royal Society|language=en}}</ref>

== Service ==
Woodruff has served on the school board of the Chicago-based [[Young Women's Leadership Charter School of Chicago|Young Women's Leadership Charter School]] and as president of [[Endocrine Society|The Endocrine Society]], and was selected as Editor-in-Chief of the journal ''[[Endocrinology (journal)|Endocrinology]]'' in September 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.endocrine.org/news-room/current-press-releases/woodruff-named-editor-in-chief-of-endocrinology|title=Woodruff named Editor-in-Chief of ''Endocrinology''|date=September 6, 2017|website=[[Endocrine Society]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180810235628/https://www.endocrine.org/news-room/current-press-releases/woodruff-named-editor-in-chief-of-endocrinology|archive-date=August 10, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=August 10, 2018|df=mdy-all}}</ref> Dr. Woodruff has also served with the Economic Club of Chicago since 2015 and as a member of the Board of Trustees of the [[Adler Planetarium]] since 2018.
